strengths: Addresses an important gap in evaluating personalization in search-augmented LLMs with a well-motivated and timely problem
Innovative dataset construction using authentic long-term user histories (2,870 sessions over 3 weeks from 30 diverse annotators) rather than synthetic personas
Novel evaluation framework combining scalar scores with diagnostic feedback on four well-chosen criteria (need alignment, content depth, tone, explanation style)
Strong meta-evaluation demonstrating high agreement with human judgments (Pearson 0.853, Spearman 0.857) and showing empirically that diagnostic feedback significantly improves evaluator quality

Comprehensive systematic analysis revealing concrete, actionable insights about user context construction (query-aware contexts outperform static; selected histories outperform raw; profiles outperform raw histories)
Excellent attention to privacy, ethics, and reproducibility with multi-stage de-identification, diverse annotators (Shannon equitability 0.91), and extensive documentation of methods and prompts
Case studies effectively demonstrate how diagnostic feedback provides detailed diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses in model responses
weaknesses: Limited scale (only 30 users, 150 queries, ~600 R-J pairs) severely constrains generalizability; findings may be specific to this small annotator cohort without evidence of broader applicability

Circular evaluation methodology: gold information is extracted from gold responses and evaluated against model responses, artificially biasing recall metrics toward confirming the gold response's completeness

Heavy and concerning dependency on GPT-5 for user context construction (Sections 4.2, C.3), oracle history selection (C.4), and evaluation (Section 3.4), making it difficult to disentangle results about personalization from model-specific artifacts

Meta-evaluation shows modest absolute performance without feedback (Pearson correlations of 0.374 for need alignment, 0.356 for content depth), and the framework appears to heavily rely on in-context examples to work well

Unclear practical impact: no model exceeds 60/100 average score despite comprehensive experiments; key findings (query-aware > static, selected > raw) are intuitive rather than surprising; no proposed methods emerge
Bi-encoder retrieval limitations (nDCG@10 = 0.082) are presented as limitations rather than solved; only one retriever model tested; query expansion helps but doesn't solve the underlying problem
Potential annotator biases: all 30 users are active daily users of Google Search and generative AI; 3-week collection window is short for capturing stable preferences; all used Google accounts

Incomplete experimental design: Table 4 shows selected configurations rather than complete factorial design; no statistical significance testing in results; GPT-5 reasoning effort always set to 'high' without justification
Limited task diversity: only 4 task types pre-selected from Search-Arena without justifying why these are the most important information-seeking scenarios for personalization
The evaluator design relies on complex manually-crafted prompts with no sensitivity analysis or ablation of prompt components; few-shot approach may not generalize beyond in-domain query-user pairs

strengths: Well-motivated evaluation of an important and timely problem in personalized search-augmented LLMs
Authentic user history collection over 3 weeks from 30 diverse annotators (Shannon equitability 0.91) is a significant empirical effort
Comprehensive four-dimensional evaluation framework (need alignment, content depth, tone, explanation style) captures nuanced personalization aspects beyond simple binary judgments
Diagnostic feedback alongside scores provides actionable signals for understanding model failures and guiding improvements
Thorough experimental analysis including meta-evaluation (0.853 correlation with human judgments), systematic ablations on context construction (Table 4), and illustrative case studies
Responsible data practices with rigorous privacy protection, de-identification, multi-stage review, and legal compliance
weaknesses: Scale is critically insufficient for a general-purpose benchmark: only 30 users and 150 test queries (1-2 orders of magnitude smaller than modern benchmarks like MMLU or HELM), raising severe generalizability concerns
Evaluation methodology depends on proprietary GPT-5 for annotation and assessment; reproducibility is compromised as the model is inaccessible and reproducibility cannot be verified independently

Meta-evaluation shows weaker-than-claimed agreement with humans: 0.461 correlation without feedback, and even with feedback only 0.853 average Pearson correlation, with need alignment specifically at 0.881, indicating substantial residual disagreement

Circular dependency in context construction: experiments require oracle LLM-based history selection (Section 4.4) to work well, but Table 5 shows real bi-encoder retrievers fail drastically (nDCG@10=0.082), making the benchmark impractical for evaluating real systems

Limited methodological novelty: evaluation framework adapts existing LLM-based evaluation techniques (Zheng et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2023) and personalization criteria from prior work (Kumar et al. 2024) without substantial innovation, and no new personalization methods are proposed

Annotation validation is incomplete: no explicit inter-annotator agreement metrics reported, only self-consistency reviews; process for generating k-1 hypothetical needs via Gemini could introduce systematic bias, and resolution of conflicting information needs is unclear

Empirical findings are intuitive (query-aware>static contexts, selective>raw history) without deep mechanistic analysis; modest improvements (need alignment 45→55 in Table 4) and no model exceeds average score of 60 without detailed root cause analysis

Missing critical analyses: no per-user or per-query-type breakdowns, no statistical significance testing, only two anecdotal examples of diagnostic feedback, no investigation of which personalization errors are most common or which user backgrounds are hardest to personalize for

Reproducibility severely compromised: dependent on proprietary APIs (GPT-5, Gemini, Perplexity), dataset not yet publicly released, all tested models are closed-source with no open-source baselines, and high cost prevents independent reproduction

Incomplete annotation documentation: gold information set construction via GPT-5 extraction + manual inspection is mentioned but impact not quantified; how many claims were manually changed? No inter-rater agreement reported for this critical step

strengths: Authentic and well-motivated benchmark addressing a clear gap in personalization evaluation for search-augmented LLMs
Comprehensive annotation methodology with 30 diverse users (Shannon equitability 0.91), long-term history collection (3 weeks), and multi-stage quality control
Strong empirical validation of LLM-based evaluator framework achieving 0.85-0.88 correlation with human judgments, with diagnostic feedback significantly improving reliability
Four well-operationalized personalization criteria (need alignment, content depth, tone, explanation style) going beyond standard factuality metrics
Thorough privacy protection with multi-stage de-identification, informed consent, ethical review, and transparent compensation procedures
Systematic experiments revealing actionable insights: query-aware > static contexts, selective > full history, structured > raw profiles
Diagnostic feedback component providing interpretable signals beyond scores, enabling targeted system improvements (Tables 10-11, Figure 3)
Excellent reproducibility with all prompts, examples, case studies, and detailed experimental protocols in appendices
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (30 users, 150 test queries) with speculative but unimplemented augmentation proposal; unclear practical scalability path
Circular validation concern: GPT-5 used for both evaluation (Er, Ep) and meta-evaluation, potentially missing systematic biases; inter-annotator agreement statistics missing
Moderate evaluator reliability: 0.88 Pearson correlation and 0.87 feedback accuracy suggest 12-13% unexplained variance; meta-evaluation on only 300 R-J pairs
Performance ceiling around 60% not adequately interpreted—unclear if benchmark is appropriately calibrated or if evaluation criteria are overly stringent
History retrieval bottleneck unresolved: bi-encoders achieve only 0.082 nDCG@10; query expansion improves to 0.38 but requires expensive LLM calls, undermining practical deployment

Limited failure mode analysis: insufficient investigation of which personalization types are fundamentally difficult, which user characteristics pose challenges, or why systems consistently underperform
Task type selection (4 of many in Search Arena) insufficiently justified; missing comparison with LaMP-QA on overlapping scenarios
Methodological novelty limited: evaluation framework adapts existing approaches; no novel algorithms proposed; contribution is primarily empirical rather than technical
Missing statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple comparison corrections on main results; unclear whether data split is cross-validated
Data availability unclear given privacy concerns with real user histories—potential barrier to community adoption; reference to code/data location is incomplete

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem in evaluating personalization of search-augmented LLMs, filling a concrete evaluation gap
Exemplary data collection: 3-week long-term human annotation with 30 diverse annotators (22+ professional domains, 60+ interests, Shannon equitability=0.91) ensuring representativeness
Rich annotation beyond simple labels: diagnostic feedback explaining scores, explicit gold information needs, multi-stage response-judgment pairs, and both search/chat histories (not just QA)
Thorough meta-evaluation demonstrating evaluator reliability: Pearson/Spearman correlations ~0.85 with humans, ablations showing feedback critical, validation with open-weight models (Appendix A.1)

Comprehensive systematic analysis with well-designed ablations (history usage, query awareness, history selection, context form) across 6 models, oracle experiments clearly identifying history inference as main bottleneck
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: extensive appendices with implementation details, prompts, case studies, dataset statistics, and clear ethical considerations with IRB approval
Practical insights: query-aware selective profiles outperform raw/static histories; reasoning models sensitive to search quality; findings actionable for system design
weaknesses: Dataset scale severely limited: only 150 queries total (30 users × 5 queries), restricting practical utility for training/evaluation; proposed LLM augmentation (A.6) not demonstrated
Evaluation methodology not novel: few-shot LLM-based evaluation follows Zheng et al. (2023) and Liu et al. (2023); application to personalization is incremental
Heavy circularity and dependence: GPT-5 used as evaluator, gold response generator, rubric generator, and profile generator, creating single point of failure; generalization beyond this model unclear
Artificial data collection: 3-week collection period with dedicated accounts is not natural long-term usage; no analysis of whether collection duration is sufficient for capturing stable preferences

Limited novelty of findings: query-aware > static profiles (intuitive), selective > full history (expected from IR), structured > raw profiles (unsurprising); no surprising insights to advance personalization research
History retrieval analysis weak: Table 5 shows ~38% recall at top-10 (nDCG 0.38); bi-encoder limitations acknowledged but not addressed; oracle uses expensive GPT-5 calls
Incomplete personalization analysis: four criteria narrow in scope; no user-segment analysis; case studies anecdotal; lacks dimensions like user satisfaction over time or trust
Statistical rigor issues: no inter-annotator agreement reported (only self-review); no significance testing; practical significance of correlation differences unexplored; limited error analysis

strengths: Rigorous data collection with long-term human annotation from 30 diverse annotators, including careful privacy protection and ethical oversight
Strong meta-evaluation demonstrating GPT-5-based evaluator achieves 0.847 Pearson correlation and 0.881 feedback accuracy with human judgments
Comprehensive ablation studies examining effects of history usage, query awareness, selective history, and profile structure on personalization
Four-criterion diagnostic feedback framework specifically designed for personalization evaluation
Honest discussion of limitations and robustness checks with open-weight models for reproducibility
Well-motivated problem addressing gap in systematic personalization evaluation for search-augmented LLMs
weaknesses: Critical scale limitations: only 30 users and 150 queries severely constrain generalizability and statistical power; meta-evaluation on 300 R-J pairs not independent from evaluator demonstrations; no inter-rater reliability or statistical significance testing reported

Questionable evaluation circularity: uses Gemini to generate hypothetical information needs, then GPT-5 to evaluate, then GPT-5-generated rubrics from Gemini-sourced examples; heavy reliance on proprietary GPT-5 model undermines reproducibility

Oracle experiment (Table 9) reveals fundamental issue—models jump from 59 to 83 need alignment with explicit preferences, suggesting benchmark primarily tests history inference rather than personalization capability, raising questions about problem formulation

Gold information recall surprisingly low (~25% even in best settings), raising concerns about gold information set quality and metric appropriateness; reasoning models catastrophically sensitive to noise (Table 6), questioning benchmark stability

Findings lack novelty—query-aware profiles outperforming static profiles, selective history outperforming full history, structured profiles outperforming raw text are all intuitive results; no surprising insights into personalization mechanisms

Limited scope: only 4 information-seeking task types, English-only, narrow user base (self-selected Google/Gemini users), 3-week history windows; unclear generalization to other personalization scenarios

Web search quality confounds evaluation—different models have different search capabilities, not fully controlled for; history retrieval still fails (nDCG@10=0.38 with query expansion), leaving major bottleneck unaddressed

Minimal actionable impact: oracle experiment identifies history inference as bottleneck but paper provides no solutions or deep investigation; no evaluation of actual personalization methods, only analysis of why current approaches fail

strengths: Realistic and diverse user dataset collected through long-term engagement with authentic chat and search histories from 30 annotators across 22+ professional domains
Comprehensive multi-stage annotation pipeline with quality control measures and validation through detailed examples (Figure 3, Tables 14-15)
Strong meta-evaluation demonstrating high alignment between GPT-5-based evaluator and human judgments (Pearson 0.847, Feedback accuracy 0.881); supplemented by open-weight model validation
Systematic ablation studies thoroughly examining four dimensions of user context construction with clear evidence that query-aware selective profiles substantially improve performance
Novel contribution of diagnostic feedback framework paired with scores, providing actionable signals for understanding personalization failures
Thorough ethical practices including multi-stage privacy review, informed consent, fair compensation ($50 + 3 months AI Pro), participant autonomy, and IRB approval
Excellent reproducibility documentation with complete prompts, annotation guidelines, dataset statistics, and commitment to release code and data
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale (30 users, 150 queries) reduces statistical robustness and generalization potential; scalability claims in Appendix A.6 via LLM augmentation remain largely speculative

Core bottleneck identified but unaddressed: oracle experiment (Appendix A.4) shows models achieve 83.47 need alignment with explicit preferences but only 59.07 with history-based inference, yet no solutions proposed
Modest technical novelty: primarily combines existing ideas (multi-level annotation, LLM-based evaluation); no new methods proposed for improving personalization
Restricted to 4 task types (analysis, guidance, recommendation, explanation); generalization to other information-seeking scenarios (factual lookup, comparison) unclear

Heavy reliance on proprietary models (GPT-5 for evaluation, Gemini for annotation) raises reproducibility and availability concerns; LLM-based PII detection and manual de-identification privacy procedures lack formal validation
Privacy procedures depend on subjective manual inspection and may miss sophisticated re-identification attacks; effectiveness of de-identification not formally validated
Some findings about user context (query-aware, selective, structured) are intuitive rather than surprising; limited methodological advancement
Key findings (oracle experiment in A.4, reasoning model sensitivity in A.5) buried in appendices despite importance; paper at 30 pages is lengthy for the contribution level
